title: Nested if vs 'and': when is each right?
idea: A nested if and an 'and' can give the same yes/no result, but a nested if lets you react differently in the middle. Predict output to see the difference.

exercises.prompt:
These two both print 'Enter' only when BOTH are True:

A) if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
       print("Enter")

B) if age >= 18:
       if has_ticket:
           print("Enter")

When only the 'Enter' case matters, which is simpler?
options: A, using 'and' - one condition, less indentation
exercises.explanation: If you only care about the all-True case, 'and' is cleaner. Nesting earns its keep when you want a DIFFERENT message in the middle.
age >= 18 is True, so we go inside. has_ticket is False, so 'Buy a ticket'. A plain 'and' could not give this middle message.

exercises.prompt: Same nested code, age = 15. What prints?
exercises.explanation: The outer if is False, so the inner ticket question is skipped and the outer else runs: 'Too young'.

exercises.prompt: Why can a nested if give THREE outcomes here while a single 'and' gives only two?
options: The nested version has an inner else AND an outer else
They always give the same number of outcomes
exercises.explanation: Each if can have its own else. Nesting stacks two choices, so you can respond to the outer-False, inner-False, and all-True cases separately.

exercises.prompt: If you only need a single yes/no result from two conditions, 'and' is usually the simpler choice.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Reach for a nested if when the in-between case needs its own response; otherwise 'and' keeps the code flat and clear.

exercises.prompt: A rule: 'Members get in free. Non-members pay, but seniors among them pay half.' Which structure fits?
options: Outer if on member; inside the non-member branch, a nested if on senior
exercises.explanation: The senior question only matters for non-members, so it belongs nested inside that branch - a choice inside a choice.
'and' combines both into one test. Use this when you don't need a separate message for the in-between case.
member is True, so the outer if runs: 'Free entry'. The nested senior check lives in the else and is skipped entirely.

exercises.prompt: Same code, member = False, age = 70. What prints?
exercises.explanation: member is False, so we enter the else. There the nested if checks age >= 65: 70 qualifies, so 'Half price'.

exercises.prompt: The lesson in one line: choose a nested if when...
options: the second question only makes sense after the first answer, and each needs its own response
you want the shortest possible code every time
two things must both be true and nothing else matters
exercises.explanation: Nesting shines when the inner question depends on the outer answer and the in-between case deserves its own branch.
